### Problem: Longest increasing subsequence {#sec-lis-p1-lis}

::: {.p-statement}
Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of `nums`.

$1 \le n \le 2500$ for the quadratic solution; the $O(n \log n)$ form handles the usual $10^5$. On $[10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]$ the answer is 4, for example $2, 3, 7, 101$. On $[0, 1, 0, 3, 2, 3]$ the answer is 4. On $[7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7]$ the answer is 1.

Source: [LC 300 · Longest Increasing Subsequence](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-increasing-subsequence/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A subsequence that ends at index $i$ has a previous end at some $j < i$ with a smaller value, or it is the single element $a[i]$. The best length ending at $i$ is one plus the best of those earlier ends. Taking the maximum only at the last index misses an LIS that ended earlier: on the first sample the length-4 chain ends at 101, and the final 18 is also length 4, but a shorter array can peak in the middle.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $end[i]$ = length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends at $i$.
- **Transition.** $end[i] = 1 + \max\{end[j] : j < i,\ a[j] < a[i]\}$.
- **Base.** $end[i] = 1$ before the loop. **Answer.** $\max_i end[i]$. **Order.** Increasing $i$.
- **Tails.** $tails[k]$ = smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length $k + 1$. Binary search replaces the first tail $\ge a_i$.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Why the tails array is sorted, and why it is not the subsequence"}
Suppose $tails[k] \ge tails[k + 1]$ after some insertion. The subsequence of length $k + 2$ ends with a value $\le$ the best end of length $k + 1$. Replacing that earlier end with this smaller value would have produced a shorter slot, which contradicts the way each slot was chosen. So the array stays strictly increasing, and the first tail that is $\ge a_i$ is found by binary search.

Overwriting a slot throws away a value that some other slot still needs. On $[10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]$ the tails finish as $[2, 3, 7, 18]$. That happens to be an LIS. Change the last step and it stops being one: the length is trustworthy, the list is not. Store the index that currently owns each slot, and the parent index that extended it, and walk the parents.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Recursion

::: {.form-next}
`f(i)` is the best increasing subsequence that ends at `i`. It tries every earlier smaller value. `f` of a first element is 1. The answer is the maximum over every ending index, because the LIS need not end at the last position.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("lis", "rec")
    assert str(final) == "4"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: lis-rec
def lis_rec(a):
    def f(i):
        best = 1
        for j in range(i):
            if a[j] < a[i]:
                best = max(best, 1 + f(j))
        return best
    return max(f(i) for i in range(len(a)))
```

##### C++

```cpp
int lisRec(int i, const vector<int>& a) {
    int best = 1;
    for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j)
        if (a[j] < a[i]) best = max(best, 1 + lisRec(j, a));
    return best;
}
```
:::

#### Memo

::: {.form-next}
There are only `n` distinct endings. `memo[i]` stores `f(i)` the first time it returns. Later calls with the same ending read the array. The body is the previous button.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("lis", "memo")
    assert str(final) == "4"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: lis-memo
def lis_memo(a):
    memo = [-1] * len(a)

    def f(i):
        if memo[i] < 0:
            best = 1
            for j in range(i):
                if a[j] < a[i]:
                    best = max(best, 1 + f(j))
            memo[i] = best
        return memo[i]

    return max(f(i) for i in range(len(a)))
```

##### C++

```cpp
int lisMemo(int i, const vector<int>& a, vector<int>& memo) {  // memo filled with -1
    if (memo[i] >= 0) return memo[i];
    int best = 1;
    for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j)
        if (a[j] < a[i]) best = max(best, 1 + lisMemo(j, a, memo));
    return memo[i] = best;
}
```
:::

#### Table

::: {.form-next}
Fill `end[i]` from the left. The recursive calls go away. A parent pointer records one `j` that achieved the maximum, and walking parents from the best index prints one LIS. The answer is still the maximum of the row, not `end[n - 1]`.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("lis", "tab")
    assert str(final) == "4"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: lis-tab
def lis_tab(a):
    n = len(a)
    end = [1] * n
    parent = [-1] * n
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i):
            if a[j] < a[i] and end[j] + 1 > end[i]:
                end[i] = end[j] + 1
                parent[i] = j
    best = max(range(n), key=lambda i: end[i])
    seq = []
    while best != -1:
        seq.append(a[best])
        best = parent[best]
    seq.reverse()
    return end[max(range(n), key=lambda i: end[i])], seq
```

##### C++

```cpp
int lisTab(const vector<int>& a, vector<int>& seq) {
    int n = a.size();
    vector<int> end(n, 1), parent(n, -1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j)
            if (a[j] < a[i] && end[j] + 1 > end[i]) {
                end[i] = end[j] + 1;
                parent[i] = j;
            }
    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i)
        if (end[i] > end[best]) best = i;
    for (int i = best; i != -1; i = parent[i]) seq.push_back(a[i]);
    reverse(seq.begin(), seq.end());
    return end[best];
}
```
:::

#### Tails

::: {.form-next}
`tails[k]` is the smallest value that ends an increasing subsequence of length `k + 1`. It stays sorted, so `a[i]` replaces the first tail that is greater than or equal to it. A brand-new slot means the LIS grew. Parents recorded at insertion reconstruct one subsequence; the tails array itself is only the length.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("lis", "tails")
    assert str(final) == "4"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: lis-tails
def lis_tails(a):
    tails, owners, parent = [], [], [-1] * len(a)
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        lo, hi = 0, len(tails)
        while lo < hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if tails[mid] >= x:
                hi = mid
            else:
                lo = mid + 1
        parent[i] = owners[lo - 1] if lo else -1
        if lo == len(tails):
            tails.append(x)
            owners.append(i)
        else:
            tails[lo] = x
            owners[lo] = i
    seq, i = [], owners[-1]
    while i != -1:
        seq.append(a[i])
        i = parent[i]
    seq.reverse()
    return len(tails), seq

def _brute_lis(a):
    best = 0
    for mask in range(1, 1 << len(a)):
        prev, length, ok = -10**18, 0, True
        for i, x in enumerate(a):
            if mask >> i & 1:
                if x <= prev:
                    ok = False
                    break
                prev, length = x, length + 1
        if ok:
            best = max(best, length)
    return best

first = [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]
assert lis_rec(first) == lis_memo(first) == 4
length, seq = lis_tab(first)
assert length == 4 and seq == [2, 5, 7, 101]
assert lis_tails(first) == (4, [2, 3, 7, 18])
assert lis_tails([0, 1, 0, 3, 2, 3])[0] == 4
assert lis_tails([7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7])[0] == 1
for _ in range(20):
    b = [random.randint(0, 6) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 8))]
    assert lis_memo(b) == lis_tab(b)[0] == lis_tails(b)[0] == _brute_lis(b)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int lisTails(const vector<int>& a) {
    vector<int> tails;
    for (int x : a) {
        int lo = 0, hi = tails.size();
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
            if (tails[mid] >= x) hi = mid;
            else lo = mid + 1;
        }
        if (lo == (int)tails.size()) tails.push_back(x);
        else tails[lo] = x;
    }
    return tails.size();
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Recursion** explores every increasing chain. **Memoisation** and the **table** are $O(n^2)$ time and $O(n)$ memory. **Tails** is $O(n \log n)$ time and $O(n)$ memory. Reconstruction adds a parent array and does not change the asymptotic time. $n \le 2500$ allows the table. $n \le 10^5$ wants tails.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- One element, or every element equal: the length is 1. Equals never extend a strict chain.
- A strictly increasing array has length $n$, and the tails array equals the array.
- A strictly decreasing array has length 1, and every insertion overwrites slot 0.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Returning `end[n - 1]`. The first sample's LIS can end at 101 or at 18; a different array peaks earlier and `end[n - 1]` is short.
- Printing `tails`. It is the smallest end of each length, overwritten as the scan moves. One real LIS is the parent walk.
- `lower_bound` on a non-decreasing problem, or `upper_bound` on a strict one. Equals must not extend a strict LIS. On seven 7s, `upper_bound` reports 7.
:::

**Variants.** Asking only whether an increasing subsequence of length 3 exists is the tails array cut down to two slots: [LC 334 · Increasing Triplet Subsequence](https://leetcode.com/problems/increasing-triplet-subsequence/){difficulty="Medium"}. Reporting the length ending at every index, with equals allowed, is the same tails scan with the first tail strictly greater than the new value: [LC 1964 · Find the Longest Valid Obstacle Course at Each Position](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-the-longest-valid-obstacle-course-at-each-position/){difficulty="Hard"}. After sorting, "divides" is a chain, and the subset is the parent walk: [LC 368 · Largest Divisible Subset](https://leetcode.com/problems/largest-divisible-subset/){difficulty="Medium"}. A weighted LIS on cake volumes is a Fenwick prefix maximum: [CF 629D · Babaei and Birthday Cake](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/629/D){rating="2000"}.
